title: IndiGo Plans Lie-Flat Business Class on A350 Fleet as Premium Long-Haul Push Accelerates
excerpt: India's largest airline is developing a dedicated business-class cabin for its 60-strong A350 order, targeting non-stop routes to London, Paris, and Frankfurt from 2027.
body:
• IndiGo is developing a dedicated business-class cabin with lie-flat seats for its Airbus A350-900 fleet, with first deliveries expected in 2027.
  • The airline has doubled its A350 order to 60 aircraft, targeting routes from Indian metros to London, Paris, Frankfurt, and Amsterdam.
  • IndiGoStretch capacity will nearly double to 4,300 seats across more than 100 A321neos, while nine additional A321XLR deliveries are planned for 2026.
  • The move marks a fundamental shift from IndiGo's low-cost origins toward a hybrid model competing directly with Air India on premium long-haul routes.

From Recliners to Lie-Flats

IndiGo, India's largest airline by market share, is developing a lie-flat business-class product for its incoming Airbus A350-900 fleet, marking the carrier's most aggressive push into premium long-haul travel. The airline has confirmed that a specialized business-class configuration is under development, though it has not disclosed specifics on seat type, cabin layout, or density.

The move represents a significant departure from the airline's current international premium offering. IndiGo's existing long-haul service, operated on wet-leased Boeing 787-9 aircraft from Norse Atlantic, features recliner seats branded as IndiGoStretch — pitched at roughly 43 inches with 12 inches of recline. While competitive at IndiGo's price points, the product falls short of the lie-flat suites offered by rivals like Air India on its new A350 and Boeing 787-9 aircraft.

That gap is set to close. The A350-900, with a maximum range exceeding 8,000 nautical miles, will give IndiGo the capability to operate non-stop from Indian metros to major European capitals — routes where passengers increasingly expect flat-bed business class on overnight flights.

A Fleet Built for Scale

IndiGo initially ordered 30 A350 aircraft in 2024 and doubled the commitment to 60 in 2025. The first deliveries are expected in 2027, with the fleet intended primarily for Europe-bound routes connecting Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, and Hyderabad to destinations including London, Paris, Frankfurt, and Amsterdam.

The airline is simultaneously expanding its narrowbody premium footprint. IndiGoStretch, first deployed on select A321neos and now on A321XLR aircraft, is being scaled to more than 100 A321neos. Business-class seat capacity across the narrowbody fleet is projected to rise from 2,800 as of March 2026 to approximately 4,300 by March 2027. Nine additional A321XLR deliveries are expected during 2026, extending IndiGo's medium-haul reach to destinations up to eight hours from India.

The A321XLR has already proven its value. IndiGo has launched routes to Athens and Istanbul, with Bali services recently announced, using the aircraft as a low-risk way to test international markets before committing widebody capacity.

"International routes could account for approximately 40% of IndiGo's network by 2030, compared with a business that historically relied heavily on domestic traffic."

— IndiGo fleet strategy outlook

The Dense Economy Question

While business class draws headlines, the A350 cabin's economy configuration may prove equally consequential. Industry analysts expect IndiGo to adopt a high-density economy layout consistent with its low-cost DNA — potentially seating well over 300 passengers in a three-class configuration with a relatively small business cabin.

Reports suggest the airline may allocate as few as 12 seats to the premium cabin, keeping the bulk of the aircraft in standard economy. This approach mirrors IndiGo's longstanding strategy of offering competitive fares through operational efficiency and high aircraft utilisation rather than premium revenue.

The challenge will be balancing yield. Air India's competing A350 configuration features 28 business-class suites with closing doors and lie-flat beds, 24 premium economy seats, and 264 economy seats — a layout designed to capture premium revenue on trunk routes. IndiGo will need to determine whether a thinner business class can generate sufficient yields to justify the A350's operating costs on competitive corridors.

What This Means for Travellers

For the Indian diaspora, particularly those flying regularly between India and Europe or North America, IndiGo's premium push introduces meaningful competition on routes long dominated by Gulf carriers and legacy airlines. The airline's combination of competitive pricing and an improving premium product could reshape pricing dynamics on key corridors.

The transition will not be immediate. IndiGo recently confirmed it will discontinue its wet-leased Norse Atlantic 787-9 operations, creating a gap before the A350 fleet arrives in 2027. During this period, the airline's long-haul ambitions will rest primarily on the A321XLR for medium-range international routes.

IndiGo's fleet backlog now exceeds 900 aircraft. Whether the airline can successfully pivot from a domestic low-cost giant to a competitive international carrier with premium aspirations remains the central question of Indian aviation's next chapter.
